newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania currency slumps before presidential polls.
newsitem.headline: Romania currency slumps before presidential polls.

text.p: The street value of Romania's leu currency on Friday plunged to below 5,000 to the dollar - the "doomsday" forecast widely dismissed only a month ago.
But the official interbank rate -- used for most trade-related transactions -- was kept far higher, further straining the country's weakened finances.

The leu, along with the battered state of Romania's economy, has been a key issue in this month's general elections amid government attempts to contain inflation and boost the currency. The second round of presidential polls is on Sunday.

Currency shops offered up to 5,050 lei per dollar - compared to just 3,500 a month ago, when the central bank scoffed at remarks by a senior banker that the currency was vastly overvalued and its true value was 5,500 to 6,000.
"The reason is quite simple. People holding dollars are in a wait and see mood and in no hurry to sell," said one currency shop owner. "But demand for dollars is quite high."
Retail traders said there could a further fall before Sunday's run-off that pits ex-communist incumbent Ion Iliescu against centrist Emil Constantinescu.
On the interbank market the dollar was worth 3,485 lei on Friday, 40 percent higher than its more realistic street value.

Operators believed pressure on the currency was only partly due to the political climate, with Constantinescu attempting to oust Iliescu and consolidate the victory of his Democratic Convention (CDR) in this month's parliamentary elections.

The CDR threw Iliescu's ex-communists out of government for the first time since the 1989 revolution. The CDR pledges to speed up market reforms and liberalise currency markets, but has not yet set specific economic targets.
Interbank traders said the leu's official value was unlikely to fall sharply next week whatever the outcome of Sunday's vote.
"The gradual slide we have seen might become a little quicker, but there won't be a sudden fall," said one trader.

Another dealer said the gap between the interbank and street rates would gradually shrink if a new government moved to liberalise markets. "I would then expect a rebound in the retail prices towards 4,500 by the end of the year," he said.
Last month Alexandru Ghiba, first Vice-President of leading bank Bancorex, forecast a drastic plunge in the value of the leu. Since then the interbank rate has slipped only 5.6 percent.

Traders struggling to clinch currency deals circumvent the official leu/dollar rate by using other currencies as a back door for trading which produce more realistic cross-rates of 4,000-4,400 lei per dollar.

The government launched its policy of controlling the leu last March by restricting the local market to four dealer banks, which posted firmer leu-dollar rates and reduced the supply of dollars to a trickle.
The International Monetary Fund cited the restrictions as one reason for suspending credits to Romania earlier this year.
Pressure on the leu is generally linked to Romania's poor economic performance.
Year-on-year inflation, reduced to 27.8 percent last year, has rebounded to 45 percent, budget and trade deficits have swelled and payment arrears almost equal the money supply.
In a bid to restore confidence the central bank recently tightened its monetary policy, raising the one-week rate for its refinancing funds to 51 from 49 percent.
Central bank chief economist Daniel Daianu last week said the outlook depended on a new cabinet having tougher policies.
"An adequate policy mix would make the forex market work, which would automatically mean a depreciation," he said.
